items.html:
Croatia has long, white licence plates. Some plates have a blue strip on the left, some are fully white. Most cars seen in Generation 3 will not feature a blue strip on their licence plates. In addition, there is a mix of cars with or without blue strips in Generation 4, with blue strips more common on newer cars.

NOTE: Blue strips are more common along the coast due to travelling tourists from other EU countries such as Italy.

Croatian bollards are white with a black rectangle and red or white reflector. From the top, it is shaped like a triangle.

NOTE: Hungarian and Lithuanian bollards look similar, but have more rounded edges compared to Croatia’s sharper edges. Lithuanian bollards will also have an orange reflector. North Macedonia sometimes uses similar bollards.

Croatian is a Slavic language. It is always written in the Latin alphabet. ‘IJE’ is common in Croatian whereas Serbian uses only ‘E’ instead.

NOTE: The Slovene language also features a lot of ‘J’s. Serbian and Montenegrin are also very similar, but Serbia and Montenegro use both Latin and Cyrillic script.
Croatia features chevrons with a red arrow on a yellow or white background.

Croatia has square (B-type) guardrails.

NOTE: Croatia is one of the few European countries that use B-type guardrails. For a good overview of European guardrails, see this infographic.

Generation 3 coverage often has a non-standard car blur where the side mirrors of the car are partially visible. This is not unique to Croatia, but by far most common there.

NOTE: Sometimes, you can see a small circular yellow sticker on the car mirror. This sticker is unique to Croatia.

Another quirk of Generation 3 coverage is that the majority of it was made in autumn. This means that the vegetation in this coverage will often have distinct yellowish or orange fall colours.

Take note that this seasonal meta is not found in Generation 4 coverage.

A black generation 4 car that will never have an antenna can be found in Croatia.

NOTE: A black car can be found in many European countries, though it will often have an antenna visible.

A white generation 4 car that will never have an antenna can be found in Croatia.

NOTE: A white car can be found in many European countries, though it will often have an antenna visible.

Stickers with the letters HR can be found on Croatian cars. HR stands for Hrvatska, the Croatian name for Croatia.

NOTE: These were mainly used before EU plates were introduced, meaning they will be less common in Generation 4.

Croatia has direction signs with a yellow background and a black outline. They often have a pencil-shaped tip.

NOTE: The other former Yugoslav countries of Slovenia, Serbia, Montenegro and North Macedonia have similar signs. A comparison can be seen here.
Croatian utility poles are cylindrical and made of concrete or wood, often with alternating hooks on the wooden poles (somewhat similar to Latvian poles).

Buildings in Croatia sometimes feature exposed red brick walls. This architecture is more common in inland areas.

NOTE: This type of architecture can also be found in Slovenia and Serbia.

Croatia features blue fire hydrants with two diagonal protrusions on either side. Newer fire hydrants seen in Generation 4 have a smaller top but are still recognisable due to the blue paint.

NOTE: Similar fire hydrants can be found in bordering countries, most commonly in Hungary.

Croatia’s pedestrian sign features a pedestrian with a belt and a zebra path with 5 stripes.

NOTE: The pedestrian on Slovenia’s sign does not have a belt.

Karlovačko and Ožujsko are common Croatian beer companies, with advertisements seen around the country.

Konzum and Plodine are common supermarket chains, mostly found in big cities. Plodine is exclusive to Croatia, while Konzum also operates stores in Bosnia.

Croatia does not have Generation 2 car coverage. However, in some historic downtown areas, a Generation 2 trekker camera was used.

NOTE: In some of this trekker coverage, the Google employee’s red cap is visible.
Croatian landlines typically start with a zero followed by the area code.
The north-eastern region of Croatia is mostly flat and features a lot of agriculture. It is similar in terms of landscape to Hungary and north-western Serbia.
The region north and west of Zagreb is hilly and agricultural.

The Adriatic coast features rocky mountains similar to those seen in Montenegro or Albania. Shrubs are more common instead of trees along the coast, especially in the south. This coastal region has a lot of islands and peninsulas.

Houses and walls made of beige brick are common on the Adriatic coast. They often feature green shutters.

NOTE: Similar architecture can also be found in some regions in Italy. Additionally, Croatian shutters can also be white, beige etc.
The north-western region of Istria, south of the Italian city of Trieste, sometimes has distinct red soil.
Bilingual street name signs with Croatian and Italian are typically found in Istria, especially in the western cities.
Town names ending with “-ec” are common to see in the northern parts of central Croatia.

Croatia’s capital Zagreb has a distinct big city feel. Apartment blocks can be seen throughout the city. The northern part of the city is hilly. Furthermore, Zagreb has blue electric trams.

NOTE: In addition to regular car coverage, Zagreb also has various urban sidewalk trekkers, often made with a Generation 2 camera.
Zagreb and Osijek are the only two cities in Croatia with trams.
The region northeast of Zadar is recognizable as it is flat with a mountain ridge visible in the distance north.

There are a lot of vineyards around the town of Ilok, near the Serbian border, west of Novi Sad. You can find vineyards in other parts of Croatia as well, but they are most common in this area. If you see lots of vineyards in a northeastern Croatian landscape, you are more often than not near Ilok.
Traffic lights in Rijeka are held up by long blue poles that extend out over the road. These are exclusive to the city.
The town of Petrinja was severely damaged by an earthquake in 2020. As a result, many buildings can be seen ruined and undergoing repair.
The city of Dubrovnik in the far south of coastal Croatia is famous for its beautifully preserved medieval city walls, which can be seen from many points in and around the Old Town.
These tall cypress trees are commonly found near the southern tip of Croatia.

steps.title: Maps and resources
steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends you play these maps instead:

  • A Balanced Croatia (map link) - 100k+ computer generated locations.
  • IntersectionGuessr - Croatia · Hrvatska (map link) - 70k+ pinpointable computer generated locations.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Croatia:

  • Plonk It Croatia (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Croatia guide from step 2 to 3.

lm.note: Bilingual street name signs with Croatian and Italian are typically found in Istria, south of the Italian city of Trieste, especially in the western cities.

lm.note: The Adriatic coast features rocky mountains similar to those seen in Montenegro or Albania. Shrubs are more common instead of trees along the coast, especially in the south. This coastal region has a lot of islands and peninsulas.

lm.name: Agricultural Hills

lm.name: East Flatland
lm.note: The north-eastern region of Croatia is mostly flat and features a lot of agriculture. It is similar in terms of landscape to Hungary and north-western Serbia.

lm.name: Istria
lm.note: The north-western region of Istria, south of the Italian city of Trieste, sometimes has distinct red soil.

lm.name: Adriatic Coast - Beige Bricks

  • They often feature green shutters.

--- NOTE:

  • This type of architecture can also be found in Slovenia and Serbia.

lm.name: Chevrons
lm.note: • Croatia features chevrons with a red arrow on a yellow or white background.

lm.name: Croatia
lm.note: Croatian landlines typically start with a zero followed by the area code. Zagreb : 01 South : 02X North : 05X(West) > 04X(Central) > 03X(East)

lm.name: Belt + Straight Legs Croatia/Bosnia
lm.note: White Belt: Croatia/Bosnia, Portugal, Germany, Hungary. > Non-Pointed Shoes: Croatia/Bosnia, Portugal. > Straight legs: Croatia/Bosnia.

lm.name: -ec town names
lm.note: Town names ending with “-ec” are common to see in the northern parts of central Croatia.

lm.name: Austrian bollards
lm.note: The island Dugi otok has lots of austrian bollards along the road.

lm.name: Beige brick walls
lm.note:
Houses and walls made of beige brick are common on the Adriatic coast. They often feature green shutters.

NOTE: Similar architecture can also be found in some regions in Italy. Additionally, Croatian shutters can also be white, beige etc.

lm.name: Blue traffic lights
lm.note: Traffic lights in Rijeka are held up by long blue poles that extend out over the road. These are exclusive to the city.

lm.name: Brod Posavina hills
lm.note: Brod Posavina and a small part of east Sisak-Moslavina is very flat and you can often see a ridge of big hills towards the north and south, sometimes the southern hills cannot be seen because of trees. The hills may also not always be directly south or north, some are a bit towards the east or west.

lm.name: Cracked pavement
lm.note:
Cracked pavement is really common in Sisak-Moslavina and to a lesser extend in Karlovac County but still common.

NOTE: Cracked pavement can ofc be found elsewhere in Croatia but these 2 regions just have the most.

lm.name: Cres and Dugi otok landscape
lm.note:
Cres and Dugi otok often feature grey/white stone walls along the road and next to it. You will also often see broken rock walls and piles of rocks laying around randomly. This is more common to see in Cres + Cres has more coverage.

These islands also mostly have gen 3 coverage.

lm.name: Croatian and Italian street name signs
lm.note: Bilingual street name signs with Croatian and Italian are typically found in Istria, especially in the western cities.

lm.name: Cypress trees
lm.note: These tall cypress trees are commonly found near the southern tip of Croatia.

lm.name: Distinct mountain ridge
lm.note: You can see this distinct big white rocky mountain ridge to the north/north-east from Kaštel Stari to Gradac. The ridge looks a bit different depending where you are but it will always be a big white rocky mountain ridge sticking out.

lm.name: Dubrovnik medieval walls
lm.note: The city of Dubrovnik in the far south of coastal Croatia is famous for its beautifully preserved medieval city walls, which can be seen from many points in and around the Old Town.

lm.name: Dubrovnik towers
lm.note: You can see these 2 towers on 2 hills in and around Dubrovnik. Sometimes you can see only 1 of the towers.

lm.name: Exposed rock
lm.note: Exposed rock is very common to see in mainland Primorje-Gorski Kotar and western Karlovac.

lm.name: Flat landscape
lm.note: The north-eastern region of Croatia is mostly flat and features a lot of agriculture. It is similar in terms of landscape to Hungary and north-western Serbia. Hills/mountains to the south can often be seen in the west and central regions.

lm.name: Flat with a mountain ridge
lm.note: The region northeast of Zadar is recognizable as it is flat with a mountain ridge visible in the distance north.

lm.name: Flat with lush green mountains and hills
lm.note:
Lika-Senj and northern Zadar provinces have flat landscapes often with random patches of trees or single trees surrounded by lush green mountains and hills, the eastern part can be a bit more hillier in terms of flatness.

NOTE: South-eastern Croatia has similar landscape but often have rocky mountains instead of lush green mountains. Also this kind of landscape can rarely appear in northern neighboring provinces aswell.

lm.name: Hilly + agricultural landscape
lm.note: The region north and west of Zagreb is hilly and agricultural.

lm.name: Ivanšćica and Medvednica
lm.note:
You can often see 2 mountains in the distance towards the south and south east in Varazdin, Krapina-Zagorje and northern Zagreb County.

Ivanšćica (south of Ivanec) is directly seen south, is alot more hillier with big elevation on the surface and has a small tower on top of it on the left side.

Medvednica (north of Zagreb) is towards the south-east, has a way flatter surface than Ivanšćica and has a bigger tower on top of it more towards the middle.

lm.name: Krk island
lm.note:
Krk island has ALOT of nice looking stone walls with stone pillar walls and fences in between them. Gardens often have lots of different kind of plants and trees in them and you can also sometimes see mountains in the distance.

The town Baška and north of it has these 2 big mountain ridges to the east and west which is very distinct.

lm.name: Krk island landscape
lm.note: The landscape in Krk is a little hilly, very green, sunny, and has this sandy/rocky white soil next to the road which you often see which is the main part that makes this island distinct. Rock walls are sometimes seen along the road aswell as mountains in the distance. The island will only have gen 4 coverage.

lm.name: Lots of vineyards
lm.note: There are a lot of vineyards around the town of Ilok, near the Serbian border, west of Novi Sad. You can find vineyards in other parts of Croatia as well, but they are most common in this area. If you see lots of vineyards in a northeastern Croatian landscape, you are more often than not near Ilok.

lm.name: Makarska mountain ridge
lm.note: Makarska has this ginormous distinct mountain ridge to the north, left side is more rocky and the right side has alot of small trees on it. Smaller towns nearby like Baška Voda and Podgora have a similar mountain ridge.

lm.name: Medvednica
lm.note: You can often see this big mountain ridge called Medvednica in City of Zagreb County and southern regions of Zagreb County. A tower on the mountain can be seen and sometimes you see tall buildings beneath it.

lm.name: Pag island
lm.note: Pag island is very rocky and dry with a distinct mountain ridge to the north-east. This sugar cane-like plant is also common on the southern half of the island and is I think really unique. Another great meta is that there is a white follow car with a red roof behind the google car, this car is seen from Rtina to Šimuni on the 106.

lm.name: Park Prirode Žumberak
lm.note: Park Prirode Žumberak is hilly and very forested, but the main thing that makes it recognizable is the large amount of brown leaves that lay on the ground along the road.

lm.name: Petrinja
lm.note: The town of Petrinja was severely damaged by an earthquake in 2020. As a result, many buildings can be seen ruined and undergoing repair.

lm.name: Požega valley
lm.note:
This valley north of Požega can be recognized by the flat and agriculture landscape with hills surrounding you from every side. The hills towards the north are the biggest.

NOTE: The hills towards the east are very small and may not always be fully visible.

lm.name: Red numbers
lm.note: Red numbers on electricity poles are most commonly found in Bjelovar-Bilogora province, especially around the city Bjelovar. Their less common in Sisak-Moslavina (most of them are around the town Popovača) and can very rarely appear in nearby provinces.

lm.name: Red soil
lm.note: The north-western region of Istria, south of the Italian city of Trieste, sometimes has distinct red soil.

lm.name: Rijeka mountains
lm.note: You can often see these big mountains to the west in and around the city Rijeka.

lm.name: Rocky mountains
lm.note: The Adriatic coast features rocky mountains similar to those seen in Montenegro or Albania. Shrubs are more common instead of trees along the coast, especially in the south. This coastal region has a lot of islands and peninsulas.

lm.name: Split
lm.note: Split, the 2nd biggest city in Croatia, is a distinct city surrounded by water, with big mountain ridges to the north and east. It has lots of big apartment buildings and 1 sky scraper which can sometimes be seen. An island can also sometimes be seen towards the west.

lm.name: Trams
lm.note:
Zagreb and Osijek are the only two cities in Croatia with trams.

Tips: Zagreb uses blue trams and busses, Osijek does not. Zagreb has a big mountain in the north, Osijek does not. Zagreb has unique street signs everywhere, Osijek does not. Zagreb in general looks alot different, its more developed with taller buildings and is hilly on some parts.

lm.name: Zagreb
lm.note:
Croatia’s capital Zagreb has a distinct big city feel. Apartment blocks can be seen throughout the city. The northern part of the city is hilly. Furthermore, Zagreb has blue electric trams and busses, it has a big mountain to the north, and has unique street name signs.

NOTE: In addition to regular car coverage, Zagreb also has various urban sidewalk trekkers, often made with a Generation 2 camera.

lm.name: Zagreb street name signs
lm.note: These 2 dark blue street signs are unique to Zagreb. It always has a white line next to the street name.

lm.name: Bollard
lm.note: Croatian bollards are white with a black rectangle and a red or white reflector. From the top, they are shaped like a triangle. Hungarian bollards are similar, but the black part with the reflector is positioned further from the top.

lm.name: Croatian
lm.note:
Croatian is the version of Serbo-Croatian official in Croatia. It is always written in the Latin script, unlike Bosnian, Montenegrin and, especially, Serbian which may use Cyrillic. Serbo-Croatian is also related to Slovene spoken in Slovenia, and may look very similar. Slovene and Serbo-Croatian both use the special characters Č, Š and Ž, but only Serbo-Croatian uses Ć and Đ aswell.

The Croatian word for street is ulica (like most Slavic languages).

Slovene and Serbo-Croatian written in Latin (South Slavic) may look similar to Czech and Slovak (West Slavic). One of the best ways to know it is a South Slavic language is to look for extensive use of letter combinations including the letter j, such as lj or nj. The Slovenian Capital of Ljubljana is a great example.

lm.name: Split
lm.note: Split, the 2nd biggest city in Croatia, is a distinct city surrounded by water, with big mountain ridges to the north and east. It has lots of big apartment buildings and 1 sky scraper which can sometimes be seen. An island can also sometimes be seen towards the west.

lm.name: Zagreb street sign
lm.note: These 2 dark blue street signs are unique to Zagreb. It always has a white line next to the street name.
